rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prefixed bi- governs what follows; its omitted complement is understood as ‘I begin’ or ‘say’ in God’s name.
rows.anchor: الباء أداة تخفض ما بعدها مثل: من وعن، والمتعلق به الباء محذوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alif is omitted from ism for ease and frequent use; al-Qutaybi explains the lengthened ba as an honorific opening, and Umar b. Abd al-Aziz ordered careful lettering.
rows.anchor: قال القتيبي ليكون افتتاح كلام كتاب الله بحرف معظم، كان عمر بن عبد العزيز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation says the ba was lengthened to mark where the omitted alif had been; the spelling keeps the alif in ‘read in the name of your Lord.’
rows.anchor: وقيل: لما أسقطوا الألف ردوا طول الألف على الباء ليكون دالا على سقوط الألف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ism can mean the named entity itself, as verses call the person Yahya by that name and call worshiped persons ‘names’; more often it means the naming.
rows.anchor: والاسم هو المسمى وعينه وذاته قال الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s naming himself in the formula teaches people how to begin recitation.
rows.anchor: قيل هو تعليم للعباد كيف يفتتحون القراءة

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad derives ism from sumuw, ‘loftiness’: the name rises above and manifests its meaning, which lies beneath it.
rows.anchor: قال المبرد من البصريين: هو مشتق من السمو وهو العلو

rows.speaker: ثعلب
rows.claim: Thaʿlab derives ism from wasm, a mark that indicates its meaning; al-Baghawi prefers the derivation from sumuw because of its diminutive and verb forms.
rows.anchor: قال ثعلب من الكوفيين: هو من الوسم والسمة وهي العلامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The derivation from sumuw is stronger: ism diminishes as sumayy, and its verb is sammaytu; a wasm derivation would yield wasīm and wasamtu.
rows.anchor: والأول أصح لأنه يصغر على السمي ولو كان من السمة لكان يصغر على الوسيم كما يقال في الوعد وعيد

rows.speaker: الخليل وجماعة
rows.claim: Al-Khalil and a group treat Allah as a proper name unique to God, with no derivation, like human proper names.
rows.anchor: قال الخليل وجماعة: هو اسم علم خاص لله عز وجل لا اشتقاق له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Others derive Allah from ilaha, worship; Ibn Abbas’s reading of ‘your gods’ as ‘your worship’ supports the sense that God alone deserves worship.
rows.anchor: اشتقاقه فقيل: من أله إلاهة أي عبد عبادة

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Al-Mubarrad connects ilah with Arabs’ phrase for finding repose in someone; a poetic line illustrates resorting to him amid calamities.
rows.anchor: قال المبرد: هو من قول العرب ألهت إلى فلان أي سكنت إليه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas calls al-Rahman and al-Rahim two tender names, one more tender than the other.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما: هما اسمان رقيقان أحدهما أرق من الآخر

rows.speaker: المبرد
rows.claim: Some treat the two names as synonyms for merciful; al-Mubarrad describes them as favor upon favor, repeated to encourage hopeful hearts.
rows.anchor: وقال المبرد: هو إنعام بعد إنعام، وتفضل بعد تفضل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A distinction makes al-Rahman’s mercy universal in this world, like provision for all, while al-Rahim’s mercy is particular to believers in the hereafter.
rows.anchor: فقال: الرحمن بمعنى العموم والرحيم بمعنى الخصوص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On this distinction, people may be called merciful (rahim) but not al-Rahman; the former is general in wording and particular in meaning, the latter opposite.
rows.anchor: فالرحمن عام المعنى خاص اللفظ، والرحيم عام اللفظ خاص المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mercy is either God’s willing good for its recipients, an attribute of essence, or withholding deserved punishment and giving unearned good, an attribute of action.
rows.anchor: والرحمة إرادة الله تعالى الخير لأهله. وقيل هي ترك عقوبة من يستحقها وإسداء الخير إلى من لا يستحق

rows.speaker: قرّاء المدينة والبصرة وفقهاء الكوفة
rows.claim: Medinan and Basran readers and Kufan jurists hold that the basmala is not part of the Fatiha or other surahs, but opens them for blessing.
rows.anchor: فذهب قراء المدينة والبصرة وفقهاء الكوفة إلى أنها ليست من فاتحة الكتاب، ولا من غيرها من السور

rows.speaker: قرّاء مكة والكوفة وأكثر فقهاء الحجاز
rows.claim: Meccan and Kufan readers and most Hijazi jurists count the basmala as part of the Fatiha only; it is written to separate surahs.
rows.anchor: وذهب قراء مكة والكوفة وأكثر فقهاء الحجاز إلى أنها من الفاتحة وليست من سائر السور وأنها كتبت للفصل

rows.speaker: الثوري وابن المبارك والشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Thawri, Ibn al-Mubarak, and al-Shafiʿi count the basmala in every surah except al-Tawba, since it is written in the codex in Quranic script.
rows.anchor: وذهب جماعة إلى أنها من الفاتحة ومن كل سورة إلا سورة التوبة وهو قول الثوري وابن المبارك والشافعي لأنها كتبت في المصحف بخط سائر القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other derivations connect the divine name with refuge and bewildered longing: creatures flee to God in hardship and need as a child turns to its mother.
rows.anchor: وقيل أصل الإله "ولاه" فأبدلت الواو بالهمزة مثل وشاح وإشاح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All agree the Fatiha has seven verses, but those counting the basmala begin the final verse at ‘those You favored’; others begin it at ‘not those under wrath.’
rows.anchor: واتفقوا على أن الفاتحة سبع آيات فالآية الأولى عند من يعدها من الفاتحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those counting the basmala cite its Quranic-script placement and a report from Ibn Abbas through Saʿid b. Jubayr: it is the seventh of the seven oft-repeated verses.
rows.anchor: هي أم القرآن قال أبي وقرأها علي سعيد بن جبير

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In the same report, Ibn Abbas says the basmala was reserved for this community and not disclosed to anyone before it.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: فذخرها لكم فما أخرجها لأحد قبلكم

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: Anas reports that Abu Bakr, Umar, and Uthman did not recite the basmala when beginning the prayer; this is evidence for excluding it from the Fatiha.
rows.anchor: عن أنس بن مالك رضي الله عنه أنه قال

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the Prophet knew a surah had ended when the basmala descended.
rows.anchor: قال سعيد بن جبير عن ابن عباس كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud says the community learned where one surah ended and another began when the basmala was revealed.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن مسعود قال: كنا لا نعلم فصل ما بين السورتين حتى ينزل بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

rows.speaker: الشعبي
rows.claim: Al-Shaʿbi traces changing opening formulas in the Prophet’s writing from ‘in your name, God’ to the complete basmala as the corresponding verses were revealed.
rows.anchor: وقال الشعبي: كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يكتب في بدء الأمر على رسم قريش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-hamd is phrased as a report that God alone deserves praise, while teaching people to say ‘praise belongs to God.’
rows.anchor: لفظه خبر كأنه يخبر أن المستحق للحمد هو الله عز وجل وفيه تعليم الخلق تقديره قولوا الحمد لله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hamd can mean gratitude for a blessing or praise for a praiseworthy quality; it is broader than thanks, since one thanks for blessings but praises knowledge or courage too.
rows.anchor: والحمد يكون بمعنى الشكر على النعمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another distinction says praise is spoken verbally while gratitude is enacted bodily.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الحمد باللسان قولا والشكر بالأركان فعلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām in lillah marks entitlement, as in saying that a house belongs to Zayd.
rows.anchor: اللام فيه للاستحقاق كما يقال الدار لزيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rabb means owner or one who nurtures and sets right; God owns and sustains all worlds, whereas a human may be called rabb only with a qualifier.
rows.anchor: فالله تعالى مالك العالمين ومربيهم، ولا يقال للمخلوق

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas defines the worlds as jinn and humans because they are morally addressed beings; the verse calls the Quran a warning to them.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: هم الجن والإنس لأنهم المكلفون بالخطاب

rows.speaker: قتادة ومجاهد والحسن
rows.claim: Qatada, Mujahid, and al-Hasan understand the worlds as all created beings, as Pharaoh’s question and Moses’ answer clarify.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة ومجاهد والحسن: هم جميع المخلوقات

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda counts four world communities—angels, humans, jinn, and devils—and excludes beasts because they do not reason.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة: هم أربع أمم: الملائكة والإنس والجن والشياطين

rows.speaker: سعيد بن المسيب
rows.claim: Saʿid b. al-Musayyab says God has one thousand worlds: six hundred in the sea and four hundred on land.
rows.anchor: قال سعيد بن المسيب لله ألف عالم ستمائة في البحر وأربعمائة في البر

rows.speaker: مقاتل بن حيان
rows.claim: Muqatil b. Hayyan says there are eighty thousand worlds, evenly divided between sea and land.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل بن حيان: لله ثمانون ألف عالم أربعون ألفا في البحر وأربعون ألفا في البر

rows.speaker: وهب
rows.claim: Wahb says there are eighteen thousand worlds and this world is only one of them, like a tent in a desert compared with the ruined land.
rows.anchor: وقال وهب لله ثمانية عشر ألف عالم الدنيا عالم منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asim, al-Kisaʾi, and Yaʿqub read malik (‘owner’); the other readers read malik (‘king’). Some regard the senses as equivalent.
rows.anchor: قرأ عاصم والكسائي ويعقوب {مالك}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation says both king and owner mean the one able to originate entities from nonexistence, a power unique to God.
rows.anchor: وقيل المالك والملك هو القادر على اختراع الأعيان من العدم إلى الوجود ولا يقدر عليه أحد غير الله

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu Ubayda prefers ‘owner’ as more comprehensive: one can own slaves, birds, and livestock, but not be king of them; ownership entails possession.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة: مالك أجمع وأوسع لأنه يقال مالك العبد والطير والدواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Others prefer ‘king’: every king is an owner, but not every owner a king, and this reading matches Quranic descriptions of God as the true King.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم: ملك أولى لأن كل ملك ملك وليس كل مالك ملكا

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid glosses din as reckoning; the phrase ‘upright din’ means an upright reckoning.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: الدين الحساب، قال الله تعالى

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومقاتل والسدي
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, Muqatil, and al-Suddi call God the judge of the day of reckoning.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس ومقاتل والسدي: ملك يوم الدين قاضي يوم الحساب

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada understands din as recompense for good and evil, as in the saying that one is repaid as one acts.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: الدين الجزاء

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب القرظي
rows.claim: Muhammad b. Kaʿb al-Qurazi says it is a day when only din benefits a person.
rows.anchor: قال محمد بن كعب القرظي: ملك يوم لا ينفع فيه إلا الدين

rows.speaker: يمان بن رباب
rows.claim: Yaman b. Rabbab derives din from subjugation: the subdued person is humbled by another’s mastery.
rows.anchor: وقال يمان بن (رباب) (1) الدين القهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The day of judgment is singled out although God owns all days because worldly sovereignties then vanish and command belongs to him alone.
rows.anchor: وإنما خص يوم الدين بالذكر مع كونه مالكا للأيام كلها لأن الأملاك يومئذ زائلة فلا ملك ولا أمر إلا له

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abu Amr assimilates the mīm in ‘al-Rahim malik’; his wider recitation rules distinguish large assimilation of moving letters from small assimilation of a silent letter into a moving one, with listed exceptions.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو: {الرحيم ملك} بإدغام الميم في الميم

rows.speaker: كعب الأحبار
rows.claim: Kaʿb al-Ahbar says no one can count the worlds except God, who alone knows his armies.
rows.anchor: وقال كعب الأحبار: لا يحصي عدد العالمين أحد إلا الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iyyaka is a pronoun used before a verb, as in ‘you alone I mean’; after a verb it appears only independently, as in ‘I meant only you.’
rows.anchor: كلمة ضمير خصت بالإضافة إلى المضمر ويستعمل مقدما على الفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worship means making God one, obeying him with humility and submission; the word for servant reflects submission, as in a trodden path.
rows.anchor: قوله {نعبد} أي نوحدك ونطيعك خاضعين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seeking help asks God’s aid for worship and all affairs; the order is challenged by those who require capacity before action, but al-Baghawi says divine enabling accompanies action.
rows.anchor: فإن قيل: لم قدم ذكر العبادة على الاستعانة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because aid is itself a kind of worship, the verse can state worship generally and then name one of its details; on his view, the ordering poses no problem.
rows.anchor: ونحن بحمد الله نجعل التوفيق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ihdina means guide us; Ali and Ubayy instead gloss it ‘keep us steadfast,’ as when someone tells a person already standing to remain so.
rows.anchor: اهدنا أرشدنا وقال علي وأبي بن كعب: ثبتنا كما يقال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers already guided ask for constancy and for further guidance, since God’s gracious aids and guidance have no limit according to Sunni doctrine.
rows.anchor: وهذا الدعاء من المؤمنين مع كونهم على الهداية بمعنى التثبيت وبمعنى طلب مزيد الهداية لأن الألطاف والهدايات من الله تعالى لا تتناهى على مذهب أهل السنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word sirat is also read with sīn, its original form; Yaʿqub’s transmitter Uways reports that reading, while zāy and Hamza’s imāla-like sound are valid dialects.
rows.anchor: وسراط بالسين رواه أويس عن يعقوب وهو الأصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers choose ṣād because it matches the written codex.
rows.anchor: والاختيار: الصاد، عند أكثر القراء لموافقة المصحف

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وجابر
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Jabir, with Muqatil, identify the straight path as Islam.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس وجابر رضي الله عنهما: هو الإسلام وهو قول مقاتل

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud identifies the path as the Quran; a report attributed to Ali from the Prophet likewise calls it God’s book.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن مسعود رضي الله عنه: هو القرآن

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿid b. Jubayr identifies the straight path as the way to Paradise.
rows.anchor: وقال سعيد بن جبير رضي الله عنه: طريق الجنة

rows.speaker: سهل بن عبد الله
rows.claim: Sahl b. Abd Allah says the path is the way of the Sunnah and community.
rows.anchor: وقال سهل بن عبد الله: طريق السنة والجماعة

rows.speaker: بكر بن عبد الله المزني
rows.claim: Bakr b. Abd Allah al-Muzani identifies it as the path of the Messenger.
rows.anchor: وقال بكر بن عبد الله المزني: طريق رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: أبو العالية والحسن
rows.claim: Abu al-Aliya and al-Hasan say it is the Messenger, his family, and his two Companions.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو العالية والحسن: رسول الله وآله وصاحباه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ordinary Arabic, sirat means a clear road.
rows.anchor: وأصله في اللغة الطريق الواضح

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: Ikrima says those favored were granted guidance and steadfastness in faith and right conduct, and identifies them as the prophets.
rows.anchor: قال عكرمة: مننت عليهم بالثبات على الإيمان والاستقامة وهم الأنبياء عليهم السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view includes all prophets and believers whom God kept firm in faith, linked with the verse describing those blessed alongside the prophets.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هم كل من ثبته الله على الإيمان

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies them as the people of Moses and Jesus before they changed their religion.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: هم قوم موسى وعيسى عليهما السلام قبل أن غيروا دينهم

rows.speaker: عبد الرحمن ابن زيد
rows.claim: Abd al-Rahman b. Zayd says they are the Prophet and those with him.
rows.anchor: وقال عبد الرحمن ابن زيد: هم النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم ومن معه

rows.speaker: أبو العالية
rows.claim: Abu al-Aliya identifies them as the Prophet’s family, Abu Bakr, and Umar.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو العالية: هم آل الرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم وأبو بكر وعمر

rows.speaker: شهر بن حوشب
rows.claim: Shahr b. Hawshab says they are the Prophet’s Companions and household.
rows.anchor: وقال شهر بن حوشب: هم أصحاب رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم وأهل بيته

rows.speaker: حمزة ويعقوب
rows.claim: Hamza reads the hāʾ of ʿalayhim, ladayhim, and ilayhim with ḍamma; Yaʿqub does so for dual and plural forms preceded by a silent yāʾ, with a stated exception.
rows.anchor: قرأ حمزة: عليهم ولديهم وإليهم بضم هاءاتها

rows.speaker: ابن كثير وأبو جعفر
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir and Abu Jaʿfar fully prolong the plural mīm in connected recitation unless a following consonant is silent; Nafiʿ may choose.
rows.anchor: وضم ابن كثير وأبو جعفر كل ميم جمع مشبعا في الوصل

rows.speaker: ورش وحمزة والكسائي وأبو عمرو ويعقوب
rows.claim: The readers differ on hāʾ and plural-mīm vowels before a hamzat al-waṣl: Warsh lengthens at hamzat al-qaṭʿ, while Hamza, al-Kisaʾi, Abu Amr, and Yaʿqub follow the stated preceding-vowel conditions.
rows.anchor: ونافع يخير، ويضم ورش عند ألف القطع، فإذا تلقته ألف وصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those under wrath are people whose path incurred God’s anger; divine anger is the will to punish sinners, but does not befall sinful believers, only disbelievers.
rows.anchor: والغضب هو إرادة الانتقام من العصاة، وغضب الله تعالى لا يلحق عصاة المؤمنين إنما يلحق الكافرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The straying ones are those who departed from guidance; the root sense of straying is perishing or disappearing, like water disappearing into milk.
rows.anchor: أي وغير الضالين عن الهدى. وأصل الضلال الهلاك والغيبوبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here ghayr functions as ‘not,’ which permits coordination with lā; if it meant ‘other than,’ such coordination would be ungrammatical.
rows.anchor: وغير هاهنا بمعنى لا ولا بمعنى غير ولذلك جاز العطف

rows.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
rows.claim: Umar’s reading says ‘the path of those You favored, not those under wrath, and not the straying ones.’
rows.anchor: وقرأ عمر بن الخطاب رضي الله عنه: صراط من أنعمت عليهم غير المغضوب عليهم وغير الضالين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reported identification makes the objects of wrath Jews and the straying ones Christians, supported by Quranic descriptions of each group.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المغضوب عليهم هم اليهود والضالون: هم النصارى

rows.speaker: سهل بن عبد الله
rows.claim: Sahl b. Abd Allah interprets those under wrath as innovators and the straying ones as people departing from the Sunnah.
rows.anchor: وقال سهل بن عبد الله: غير المغضوب {عليهم} (1) بالبدعة، ولا الضالين عن السنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reciter should say Amin after a separate pause; the word is normally light, though grammarians allow a long or short vowel, and means ‘God, hear and answer.’
rows.anchor: والسنة للقارئ أن يقول بعد فراغه من قراءة الفاتحة "آمين" بسكتة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وقتادة
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Qatada gloss Amin as ‘so be it.’
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس وقتادة: معناه كذلك يكون

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says Amin is one of God’s names.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد هو اسم من أسماء الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other explanations call Amin the seal of a supplication or God’s seal protecting servants from harm, like a seal protecting a letter.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هو طابع الدعاء. وقيل هو خاتم الله على عباده يدفع به الآفات عنهم

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة
rows.claim: Abu Hurayra reports that when the imam says Amin, worshippers should do so too; angels also say it, and agreement with them brings forgiveness of past sins. Al-Baghawi grades it sound.
rows.anchor: عن أبي هريرة رضي الله عنه أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال: "إذا قال الإمام

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas says that when the Prophet recited ‘Glorify the name of your Lord Most High,’ he said ‘Glory to my Lord Most High’; a group of Companions and Successors agree.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قرأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some understand the command as declaring God above the descriptions of heretics and treat ‘name’ as an extra word; this supports identifying name and named entity.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم: معناه نزه ربك الأعلى عما يصفه به الملحدون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Others interpret it as honoring the naming of God by remembering him reverently and obeying his commands, taking ism to mean naming or mention.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون: نزه تسمية ربك، بأن تذكره وأنت له معظم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas also interprets the command as praying according to the order of the Most High Lord.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: سبح [اسم ربك الأعلى] (2) أي:

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says God created every living being and proportioned its hands, feet, and eyes.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: خلق كل ذي روح، فسوى اليدين والرجلين والعينين

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says God created humans upright and proportioned their stature.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: خلق الإنسان مستويا،

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisaʾi reads qaddara with a light dāl; the other readers geminate it, and both forms mean the same.
rows.anchor: قرأ الكسائي: "قدر" بتخفيف الدال

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says God guided humans to good and evil and to felicity or misery, and guided livestock to their pastures.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: هدى الإنسان لسبيل الخير والشر

rows.speaker: مقاتل والكلبي
rows.claim: Muqatil and al-Kalbi say God assigned every thing its course and showed animals how to mate.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل والكلبي: قدر لكل شيء مسلكه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says God apportioned provisions and guided creatures to earn their livelihood.
rows.anchor: وقيل: قدر الأرزاق وهدى لاكتساب الأرزاق والمعاش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says God created benefits in things and guided people to discover how to extract them.
rows.anchor: وقيل: خلق المنافع في الأشياء، وهدى الإنسان لوجه استخراجها منها

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says God determined the embryo’s term in the womb and then guided it out.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: قدر مدة الجنين في الرحم ثم هداه للخروج من الرحم

rows.speaker: الواسطي
rows.claim: Al-Wasiti says God predetermined bliss and misery, then made each group follow the path assigned to it.
rows.anchor: قال الواسطي: قدر السعادة والشقاوة عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-marʿa is the grass God grows for grazing animals, in green, yellow, red, and white varieties.
rows.anchor: أنبت العشب وما ترعاه [النعم] (4) من بين أخضر وأصفر وأحمر وأبيض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After it is green, God makes the pasture dry, decayed, and black, like foam floating on a torrent.
rows.anchor: هشيما باليا، كالغثاء الذي تراه فوق السيل

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says God will make the Prophet’s work easy for Paradise; Ibn Abbas’s gloss similarly says he will be enabled to do good, with ‘the easier way’ meaning good works.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل: نهون عليك عمل أهل الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view takes the phrase to mean that God will grant the Prophet the easy, tolerant monotheistic law.
rows.anchor: وقيل: نوفقك للشريعة اليسرى وهي الحنيفية السمحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A contextual reading links the promise to revelation: God will ease the Prophet’s recitation, memory, and teaching of what he receives from Gabriel.
rows.anchor: ثم وعده فقال: {ونيسرك لليسرى} أي نهون عليك الوحي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is to admonish with the Quran; ‘if the reminder benefits’ means whether it benefits or not, with the second possibility omitted as in a verse that mentions protection from heat but implies cold too.
rows.anchor: والمعنى: نفعت أو لم تنفع، وإنما لم يذكر الحالة الثانية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The one who will take heed is the person who fears God.
rows.anchor: يتعظ {من يخشى} الله عز وجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The most wretched person, in God’s foreknowledge, will shun and distance himself from the reminder.
rows.anchor: أي يتجنب الذكرى ويتباعد عنها {الأشقى} الشقي في علم الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ‘greatest fire’ is immense and dreadful, hotter and more severe than the fire of this world.
rows.anchor: العظيمة والفظيعة، لأنها أعظم وأشد حرا من نار الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people of the fire neither die and find relief nor live a life that benefits them.
rows.anchor: فيستريح {ولا يحيا} حياة تنفعه

rows.speaker: عطاء وعكرمة وابن عباس وسعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Ata, Ikrima, and reports from Ibn Abbas and Saʿid b. Jubayr say the successful person purifies himself from idolatry and professes that there is no god but God.
rows.anchor: تطهر من الشرك وقال: لا إله إلا الله. هذا قول عطاء وعكرمة، ورواية الوالبي وسعيد بن جبير عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says the successful person is one whose deeds are righteous.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: من كان عمله زاكيا

rows.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
rows.claim: Another interpretation is alms at the end of Ramadan; Abu Saʿid al-Khudri reports that ‘he purified himself’ means paying the fitr charity.
rows.anchor: روي عن أبي سعيد الخدري

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: A reading links remembering God’s name and prayer with going out for the Eid prayer after giving charity; Ibn Masud prayed for the one who gives then prays.
rows.anchor: فكان ابن مسعود يقول: رحم الله امرءا تصدق ثم صلى

rows.speaker: ابن عمر
rows.claim: Nafiʿ reports that Ibn Umar checked whether charity had been given before going to the prayer ground, connecting the verses to charity and Eid prayer; Abu al-Aliya and Ibn Sirin hold this view.
rows.anchor: وروى نافع: كان ابن عمر إذا صلى الغداة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some object that the surah is Meccan, before Eid or fitr charity existed; al-Baghawi replies that revelation can precede the ruling, as with the Prophet’s lawful entry into Mecca and the prophecy of Badr.
rows.anchor: يجوز أن يكون النزول سابقا على الحكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Remembering God may mean the Eid takbirs and prayer the Eid prayer; another view takes ṣalla here to mean supplication.
rows.anchor: قيل: الذكر: تكبيرات العيد، والصلاة: صلاة العيد

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو ويعقوب
rows.claim: Abu Amr and Yaʿqub read ‘they prefer’ in the third person, referring to the wretched people mentioned; other readers address the audience directly.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو عمرو، ويعقوب: [يؤثرون] (1) بالياء

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: Ubayy’s reading says ‘rather, you prefer the worldly life,’ supporting the direct-address reading; al-ashqa is singular in form but generic and plural in reference.
rows.anchor: دليله: قراءة أبي بن كعب "بل أنتم تؤثرون الحياة الدنيا"

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud explains that people prefer this life because its food, drink, women, pleasures, and beauty are immediate, while the hereafter is described but kept from them.
rows.anchor: قال عرفجة الأشجعي: كنا عند ابن مسعود فقرأ هذه الآية، فقال لنا: أتدرون لم آثرنا الحياة الدنيا على الآخرة؟ قلنا: لا قال: لأن الدنيا أحضرت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘This’ refers to the preceding four verses: the earlier scriptures taught that the purified and praying prosper, people favor worldly life, and the afterlife is better and more lasting.
rows.anchor: ما ذكر من قوله: "قد أفلح من تزكى"

rows.speaker: عكرمة والسدي
rows.claim: Ikrima and al-Suddi say this entire surah is found in the scrolls of Abraham and Moses.
rows.anchor: قال عكرمة والسدي: هذه السورة في صحف إبراهيم وموسى

rows.speaker: عائشة
rows.claim: Aisha reports that the Prophet recited al-Aʿla and al-Kafirun in the two rakʿas before witr, then al-Ikhlas, al-Falaq, and al-Nas in witr.
rows.anchor: عن عائشة رضي الله عنها قالت: كان النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم يقرأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report of the Overwhelming Event is the account of the Resurrection, whose terrors engulf everything.
rows.anchor: يعني: قد أتاك حديث القيامة، تغشى كل شيء بالأهوال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The faces on that day are humbled and abased.
rows.anchor: يعني: يوم القيامة {خاشعة} ذليلة

rows.speaker: عطاء عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ata from Ibn Abbas says the people exerted themselves in worldly work outside Islam—idolaters and disbelievers among the People of the Book, including monks—yet their effort in error is rejected and they enter Hell; naṣab means toil.
rows.anchor: قال عطاء عن ابن عباس: يعني الذين عملوا ونصبوا في الدنيا

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير وزيد بن أسلم
rows.claim: Saʿid b. Jubayr and Zayd b. Aslam share the view that these people labored in worldly disbelief and their effort is rejected.
rows.anchor: وهو قول سعيد بن جبير، وزيد بن أسلم. ومعنى النصب: الدأب في العمل بالتعب

rows.speaker: عكرمة والسدي
rows.claim: Ikrima and al-Suddi say they sinned in this world and will toil in the next.
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة والسدي: عاملة في الدنيا بالمعاصي، ناصبة في الآخرة في النار

rows.speaker: الحسن وقتادة وابن عباس
rows.claim: Another view, held by al-Hasan and Qatada and reported from Ibn Abbas, says they work and toil in Hell; chains and shackles make them labor because they did not work for God in life.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن: لم تعمل لله في الدنيا، فأعملها وأنصبها في النار

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masud says they wade through fire as camels wade through mud.
rows.anchor: قال ابن مسعود: تخوض في النار كما تخوض الإبل في الوحل

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says the inhabitants are dragged over their faces in Hell.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: يجرون على وجوههم في النار

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak says they are made to climb a mountain of iron in Hell.
rows.anchor: [وقال الضحاك: يكلفون ارتقاء جبل من حديد في النار]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording speaks of faces but refers to the people who bear them.
rows.anchor: والكلام خرج على "الوجوه" والمراد منها أصحابها

rows.speaker: أهل البصرة وأبو بكر
rows.claim: Basran readers and Abu Bakr read tuṣlā with a ḍamma on the tāʾ, matching ‘they are given to drink’; others read it with fatḥa.
rows.anchor: قرأ أهل البصرة وأبو بكر: "تصلى" بضم التاء

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the blazing fire has become intensely hot and flares against God’s enemies.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: قد حميت فهي تتلظى على أعداء الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The spring is at its utmost heat, kindled over Hell since its creation; the condemned are driven to it thirsty.
rows.anchor: متناهية في الحرارة قد أوقدت عليها جهنم منذ خلقت، فدفعوا إليها

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The commentators say a drop from that spring would melt the mountains of this world.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون: لو وقعت منها قطرة على جبال الدنيا لذابت

rows.speaker: مجاهد وعكرمة وقتادة
rows.claim: Mujahid, Ikrima, and Qatada identify ḍariʿ as a low-growing thorn plant called shibriq by Quraysh while green and ḍariʿ once dry; it is foul food.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد وعكرمة وقتادة: هو نبت ذو شوك لاطئ بالأرض

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says no animal approaches the plant once it is dry.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: لا تقربه دابة إذا يبس

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says worldly ḍariʿ is dry thorn with withered leaves, while the afterlife version is thorn made of fire.
rows.anchor: قال ابن زيد: أما في الدنيا فإن "الضريع" الشوك اليابس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report from Ibn Abbas describes the Hell thorn as more bitter than aloes, fouler than carrion, and hotter than fire.
rows.anchor: وجاء في الحديث عن ابن عباس: "الضريع: شيء في النار

rows.speaker: أبو الدرداء والحسن
rows.claim: Abu al-Darda and al-Hasan report that God afflicts Hell’s inhabitants with hunger; after ḍariʿ and choking food they beg for water, remain thirsty a thousand years, then boiling water peels faces and cuts their entrails, as in the cited verse.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو الدرداء، والحسن: إن الله تعالى يرسل على أهل النار الجوع

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: The commentators say polytheists objected that their camels fatten on ḍariʿ, but camels eat it only while green; dry shibriq is eaten by nothing, so it gives no nourishment or relief.
rows.anchor: قال المفسرون: فلما نزلت هذه الآية قال المشركون: إن إبلنا لتسمن على الضريع

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says the blessed faces are in comfort and honor.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل: في نعمة وكرامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They are pleased in the afterlife with their worldly striving when rewarded with Paradise.
rows.anchor: في الدنيا {راضية} في الآخرة حين أعطيت الجنة بعملها

rows.speaker: أهل مكة والبصرة ونافع
rows.claim: Meccan and Basran readers use a passive third-person ‘no vain speech is heard’ with nominative laghiya; Nafiʿ uses feminine passive with nominative; other readers use feminine active and accusative, addressing the Prophet.
rows.anchor: قرأ أهل مكة والبصرة: "لا يسمع" بالياء وضمها، "لاغية" رفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Paradise contains a flowing spring.
rows.anchor: فيها عين جارية

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the elevated couches have gold boards adorned with gems; they lower for a person to sit and rise again afterward.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: ألواحها من ذهب مكللة بالزبرجد والدر والياقوت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cups are set out nearby; a kub is a pitcher without a handle.
rows.anchor: عندهم، جمع كوب، وهو الإبريق الذي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Namariq are cushions and pillows lined beside one another.
rows.anchor: وسائد ومرافق {مصفوفة} بعضها بجنب بعض

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies the zarabi as plush carpets spread out; another gloss says they are scattered among the sitting places.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: هي الطنافس التي لها خمل

rows.speaker: أهل التفسير
rows.claim: The commentators say God names the camel after unbelievers marvel at and deny the promised Paradise: he recalls his worldly creation of their livelihood and will create what he has promised there.
rows.anchor: قال أهل التفسير: لما نعت الله تعالى في هذه السورة ما في الجنة

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says camels were singled out because Arabs had seen no larger beast, while only a few had seen an elephant.
rows.anchor: فقال مقاتل: لأنهم لم يروا بهيمة قط أعظم منها

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi highlights that camels rise while carrying their load after kneeling.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: لأنها تنهض بحملها وهي باركة

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says people wondered how they would climb the raised couches of Paradise, so God pointed to the camel’s creation.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: ذكر الله تعالى ارتفاع سرر الجنة وفرشها

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan argues the elephant was remote and useless to Arabs for riding, meat, or milk, whereas camels are their most precious property, eat date stones and fodder, and give milk.
rows.anchor: وسئل الحسن عن هذه الآية، وقيل له: الفيل أعظم في الأعجوبة؟ فقال: أما الفيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation stresses the camel’s size together with its docility: even a small child can lead it where he wants.
rows.anchor: وقيل: [إنها] (3) مع عظمها تلين للحمل الثقيل وتنقاد للقائد الضعيف

rows.speaker: شريح القاضي
rows.claim: Judge Shurayh used to take people out to a camel stable to observe how camels were created.
rows.anchor: وكان شريح القاضي يقول: اخرجوا بنا إلى [كناسة اسطبل]

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sky was raised above the earth without anything supporting it.
rows.anchor: عن الأرض حتى لا ينالها شيء بغير عمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mountains were set firmly on the earth so they do not move.
rows.anchor: على وجه الأرض [مرساة] (6) لا تزول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earth was spread flat; Ata reports Ibn Abbas’s rhetorical challenge that no one but God can create camels, raise the sky, set mountains, or spread earth.
rows.anchor: قال عطاء عن ابن عباس: هل يقدر أحد أن يخلق مثل الإبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is to remind people, not exercise control by killing them or forcing them to believe; al-Baghawi says the fighting verse abrogated this rule.
rows.anchor: [أي: عظ يا محمد] (1) {إنما أنت مذكر لست عليهم بمسيطر}

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception is disconnected: ‘but’ the one who turns away and disbelieves after being reminded.
rows.anchor: استثناء منقطع عما قبله، معناه: لكن من تولى وكفر بعد التذكير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The greater punishment is entry into Hell; it is called greater because they already endured hunger, drought, killing, and captivity in this world.
rows.anchor: لأنهم عذبوا في الدنيا بالجوع والقحط والقتل والأسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their return means their coming back after death; the root āba means to return.
rows.anchor: رجوعهم بعد الموت، يقال آب يؤب أوبا وإيابا

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر
rows.claim: Abu Jaʿfar unusually geminates the yāʾ in iyābahum; al-Zajjaj alone accepts it, deriving it from ayaba on the pattern fiʿāla.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو جعفر: "إيابهم" بتشديد الياء، وهو شاذ لم يجزه أحد غير الزجاج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After they return to God, their reckoning means their recompense.
rows.anchor: يعني جزاءهم بعد المرجع إلى الله عز وجل

rows.speaker: حمزة والكسائي
rows.claim: Hamza and al-Kisaʾi pronounce watr with a kasra on the wāw; the other readers use fatḥa.
rows.anchor: قرأ حمزة، والكسائي: "الوتر" بكسر الواو، وقرأ الآخرون بفتحها

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود وأبو سعيد الخدري وعطية العوفي
rows.claim: One view identifies the paired as creation and the single as God; it is reported from Ibn Masud, Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, and held by Atiyya al-Awfi.
rows.anchor: و"الوتر" هو الله عز وجل. روي ذلك عن [ابن مسعود وعن] (1) أبي سعيد الخدري، وهو قول عطية العوفي

rows.speaker: مجاهد ومسروق
rows.claim: Mujahid and Masruq say all creation is paired, including opposites such as belief and unbelief, guidance and error, heaven and earth, while God is uniquely one.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد ومسروق: "الشفع" الخلق كله

rows.speaker: الحسن وابن زيد
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd say all creation includes both even and odd kinds.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن وابن زيد: "الشفع والوتر" الخلق كله، منه شفع، ومنه وتر

rows.speaker: قتادة عن الحسن
rows.claim: Qatada reports from al-Hasan that paired and single refer to numbers, some even and some odd.
rows.anchor: وروى قتادة عن الحسن قال: هو العدد منه شفع ومنه وتر

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says they are the prayers, some consisting of an even number and some an odd one; a marfuʿ report from Imran b. Husayn also gives this view.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: هما الصلوات منها شفع ومنها وتر. وروى ذلك عن عمران بن حصين مرفوعا

rows.speaker: عطية عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ata reports Ibn Abbas’s view that the paired is the dawn prayer and the single the sunset prayer.
rows.anchor: وروى عطية عن ابن عباس: الشفع صلاة الغداة، والوتر صلاة المغرب

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن الزبير
rows.claim: Ibn al-Zubayr identifies the paired and single with the first and last days of pilgrimage, citing the rule for departing in two or three days.
rows.anchor: وعن عبد الله بن الزبير قال: "الشفع" يوم النفر الأول، و"الوتر" يوم النفر الأخير

rows.speaker: مقاتل بن حيان
rows.claim: Muqatil b. Hayyan says the paired are days and nights and the single is the Day of Resurrection, after which there is no night.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل بن حيان: "الشفع" الأيام والليالي، و"الوتر" اليوم الذي لا ليلة بعده

rows.speaker: الحسين بن الفضل
rows.claim: Al-Husayn b. al-Fadl says the paired are Paradise’s eight ranks and the single is Hell’s seven levels.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسين بن الفضل: "الشفع" درجات الجنة لأنها ثمان، و"الوتر" دركات النار لأنها سبع

rows.speaker: أبو بكر الوراق
rows.claim: Abu Bakr al-Warraq sees paired opposites in created beings but divine attributes as singly perfect: might without humiliation, power without incapacity, knowledge without ignorance, and life without death.
rows.anchor: وسئل أبو بكر الوراق عن الشفع والوتر فقال: "الشفع" تضاد [أخلاق] (2) المخلوقين

rows.speaker: قتادة ومجاهد والكلبي وابن عباس
rows.claim: Ad were called ‘possessors of pillars’ because they lived in traveling tents; this is held by Qatada, Mujahid, al-Kalbi, and reported from Ibn Abbas.
rows.anchor: وسموا ذات العماد [لهذا] (2) لأنهم كانوا أهل عمد سيارة، وهو قول قتادة ومجاهد والكلبي، ورواية عطاء عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومقاتل
rows.claim: Another view derives the name from their great stature: Ibn Abbas compares them to pillars and Muqatil says each was twelve cubits tall.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يعني طولهم مثل العماد. وقال مقاتل: كان طول أحدهم اثني عشر ذراعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No tribe like them existed in height and strength; they said, ‘Who is stronger than us?’
rows.anchor: أي لم يخلق مثل تلك القبيلة في الطول والقوة، وهم الذين قالوا: "من أشد منا قوة"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further view says they were named for an immense building raised by one of them: Shaddad built an unmatched city and was destroyed with his party before reaching it.
rows.anchor: يقال: بناه شداد بن عاد على صفة لم يخلق في الدنيا مثله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thamud cut stone in the valley, carving homes into mountains; the valley is identified as Wadi al-Qura.
rows.anchor: أي: وبثمود، {الذين جابوا الصخر} قطعوا الحجر، واحدتها: صخرة، {بالواد} يعني [وادي القرى] (4)

rows.speaker: ابن كثير ويعقوب وورش
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir and Yaʿqub retain the yāʾ in al-wadi in both pause and connection; Warsh retains it only in connection, while the others omit it.
rows.anchor: وأثبت ابن كثير ويعقوب الياء في الوادي وصلا ووقفا على الأصل، وأثبتها ورش وصلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pharaoh was called ‘of the stakes’ because he tortured people with stakes; the account is also treated in Surat Sad.
rows.anchor: سمي بذلك لأنه كان يعذب الناس بالأوتاد، وقد ذكرناه في سورة (ص)

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A lengthy report from Ibn Abbas says Pharaoh’s treasurer Hizbil was a hidden believer; his wife, Pharaoh’s daughter’s hairdresser, professed one God, endured four stakes, snakes, and scorpions rather than recanting, and her infant spoke of her heavenly home before being killed.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس: أن فرعون إنما سمي "ذي الأوتاد" لأنه كانت امرأة، وهي امرأة خازن فرعون حزبيل

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: The same report says Hizbil escaped; when Pharaoh’s agents found him praying with rows of beasts, one hid the encounter and later believed while the other exposed it, received a reward, and was killed and crucified.
rows.anchor: فبعث رجلين في طلبه فانتهيا إليه وهو يصلي ويليه صفوف من الوحوش خلفه يصلون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The transgressors were Ad, Thamud, and Pharaoh, who disobeyed and behaved arrogantly in the land.
rows.anchor: يعني عادا وثمود وفرعون، عملوا في الأرض بالمعاصي وتجبروا

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada glosses the lash of punishment as a kind or variety of punishment poured on them.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة: يعني لونا من العذاب صبه عليهم

rows.speaker: أهل المعاني
rows.claim: The scholars of meaning call ‘lash’ a metaphor: because a whip is an extreme punishment, the term stands for every kind of torment.
rows.anchor: قال أهل المعاني: هذا على الاستعارة، لأن السوط عندهم غاية العذاب، فجرى ذلك لكل نوع من العذاب

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says God made the punishment itself his whip with which he struck them.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: جعل سوطه الذي ضربهم به العذاب

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says God is at the watchpoint, seeing, hearing, and observing.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: يعني بحيث يرى ويسمع ويبصر

rows.speaker: الكلبي ومقاتل
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi and Muqatil describe the watchpoint as the road of servants, from which no one escapes.
rows.anchor: قال الكلبي: عليه طريق العباد لا يفوته أحد. قال مقاتل: ممر الناس عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that all creatures return to God’s judgment and command, and to him they ultimately go.
rows.anchor: وقيل: مرجع الخلق إلى حكمه وأمره وإليه مصيرهم

rows.speaker: الحسن وعكرمة
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and Ikrima say God watches the deeds of human beings.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن وعكرمة: يرصد أعمال بني آدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The point is that no deed escapes God, just as no one escapes a person stationed at a watchpoint.
rows.anchor: والمعنى: أنه لا يفوته شيء من أعمال العباد، كما لا يفوت من هو بالمرصاد

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says God placed the fire on their route to destroy them.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: أرصد الله النار على طريقهم حتى يهلكهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The person calls wealth an honor and poverty a humiliation; qaddara is read with geminated dāl by Abu Jaʿfar and Ibn Amir, ungeminated by others, and both forms mean to restrict provision.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو جعفر وابن عامر "فقدر" بتشديد الدال، وقرأ الآخرون بالتخفيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another lexical gloss takes qaddara as ‘gave sparingly,’ allotting only what suffices.
rows.anchor: وقيل: "قدر" بمعنى قتر وأعطاه قدر ما يكفيه

rows.speaker: الكلبي ومقاتل
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi and Muqatil say this disbelieving complaint was revealed about Umayya b. Khalaf, who equated wealth with honor and poverty with disgrace.
rows.anchor: وهذا يعني به الكافر، تكون الكرامة والهوان عنده بكثرة المال والحظ في الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God rejects the equation: wealth and poverty are his allotment, not measures of honor; he may enrich an unbeliever or restrict a believer, honoring through obedience and disgracing through sin.
rows.anchor: فأخبر أن الإكرام والإهانة لا تدور على المال وسعة الرزق، ولكن الفقر والغنى بتقديره

rows.speaker: أهل الحجاز والبصرة وابن كثير ويعقوب
rows.claim: Hijazi and Basran readers retain the final yāʾ of akramani and ahanani in connected recitation; Ibn Kathir and Yaʿqub retain it also at a pause, while others omit it.
rows.anchor: قرأ أهل الحجاز والبصرة "أكرمني وأهانني" بإثبات الياء في الوصل

rows.speaker: أهل البصرة
rows.claim: Basran readers use third-person yāʾ in the four verbs; others address the audience with tāʾ.
rows.anchor: قرأ أهل البصرة: "يكرمون، ويحضون، ويأكلون، ويحبون" بالياء فيهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Failing to honor an orphan means either treating the orphan well inadequately or withholding the orphan’s due.
rows.anchor: لا تحسنون إليه. وقيل: لا تعطونه حقه

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says Qudama b. Mazʿun was an orphan in Umayya b. Khalaf’s care, and Umayya denied him his right.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل: كان قدامة بن مظعون يتيما في حجر أمية بن خلف وكان يدفعه عن حقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They do not urge others to feed the poor.
rows.anchor: أي لا تأمرون بإطعامه

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر وأهل الكوفة
rows.claim: Abu Jaʿfar and Kufan readers vocalize taḥāḍḍūna with an open ḥāʾ and a following alif, meaning people do not urge one another to feed the poor.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو جعفر وأهل الكوفة: "تحاضون" بفتح الحاء وألف بعدها، أي لا يحض بعضكم بعضا عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The tranquil soul trusts God’s promise and affirms what God has said.
rows.anchor: إلى ما وعد الله عز وجل المصدقة بما قال الله

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid calls it the soul that knows God is its Lord and patiently remains firm in his command and obedience.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: "المطمئنة" التي أيقنت أن الله تعالى ربها وصبرت جأشا لأمره وطاعته

rows.speaker: الحسن وعطية والكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Hasan calls it the certain believer, Atiyya the soul content with God’s decree, and al-Kalbi the soul safe from God’s punishment.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: المؤمنة الموقنة، وقال عطية: الراضية بقضاء الله تعالى. وقال الكلبي: الآمنة من عذاب الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is a soul reassured by remembrance of God, as in the verse that says hearts find reassurance in remembering God.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المطمئنة بذكر الله، بيانه:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say the address comes at death: the soul is told to return to God, pleased with its reward and pleasing to him.
rows.anchor: فقال قوم: يقال لها ذلك عند الموت فيقال لها:

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says that as God takes the soul, it becomes at peace with and content toward God, and God is pleased with it.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: إذا أراد الله قبضها اطمأنت إلى الله ورضيت عن الله ورضي الله عنها

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو
rows.claim: Ibn Amr reports that a believing soul is greeted at death, leaves fragrant, passes through opened heavenly doors while angels pray for it, prostrates before God, and is placed among believers; its grave is widened and lit, while the unbeliever is sent out foul to wrath and Hell.
rows.anchor: قال عبد الله بن عمرو: (1) إذا توفي العبد المؤمن أرسل الله عز وجل ملكين إليه

rows.speaker: أبو صالح
rows.claim: Abu Salih says ‘return to your Lord’ is spoken when the soul leaves worldly life, while ‘enter among my servants and enter my Paradise’ is spoken at resurrection.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو صالح في قوله: "ارجعي إلى ربك راضية مرضية" قال: هذا عند خروجها من الدنيا

rows.speaker: عكرمة وعطاء والضحاك وابن عباس
rows.claim: Others, including Ikrima, Ata, al-Dahhak, and a report from Ibn Abbas, say the soul is addressed at resurrection and ordered back to its body.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون: إنما يقال لها ذلك عند البعث يقال: ارجعي [إلى ربك] (3)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Entering among God’s servants means joining them in Paradise; another view specifies the obedient, chosen, righteous servants, as in the prayer to be admitted among the righteous.
rows.anchor: أي مع عبادي في جنتي. وقيل: في جملة عبادي الصالحين المطيعين المصطفين

rows.speaker: أهل الإشارة
rows.claim: Some mystically interpret the tranquil soul as attached to worldly life, told to return to God by abandoning it and following the path of the afterlife.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض أهل الإشارة: يا أيتها النفس المطمئنة إلى الدنيا ارجعي إلى الله بتركها

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿid b. Jubayr recounts Ibn Abbas’s funeral: a strange bird entered the bier and never emerged, and the full ‘tranquil soul’ verses were recited at the grave by an unknown voice.
rows.anchor: وقال سعيد بن جبير: مات ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما بالطائف فشهدت جنازته، فجاء طائر لم [نر] (1)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: La uqsim is affirmative: ‘I swear’ by Mecca.
rows.anchor: يعني، أقسم {بهذا البلد} يعني مكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is made lawful in Mecca to do what he wills, including fighting and capture, which are forbidden to others; God permitted this on the conquest.
rows.anchor: أي حلال، {بهذا البلد} تصنع فيه ما تريد من القتل والأسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the conquest, the Prophet fought and ordered Ibn Khatal and others killed, while promising safety to those who entered Abu Sufyan’s house; he then said Mecca was sacred from creation and was permitted to him for one hour only.
rows.anchor: أحل الله تعالى لنبيه صلى الله عليه وسلم مكة يوم الفتح، حتى قاتل وقتل وأمر بقتل ابن خطل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The oath displays Mecca’s great rank despite its sanctity, and promises that God would permit the Prophet to fight there and conquer it.
rows.anchor: والمعنى: أن الله تعالى لما أقسم بمكة دل ذلك على عظيم قدرها مع حرمتها، فوعد نبيه صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: شرحبيل بن سعد
rows.claim: Sharhabil b. Saʿd instead says that people protect game in Mecca but regard it as lawful to expel or kill the Prophet there.
rows.anchor: قال شرحبيل بن سعد: ومعنى قوله: "وأنت حل بهذا البلد" قال: يحرمون أن يقتلوا بها صيدا

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير وقتادة
rows.claim: Saʿid b. Jubayr and Qatada say the person thinks God neither sees him nor will ask where his wealth came from or where he spent it.
rows.anchor: قال سعيد بن جبير [وقتادة: أيظن] (1) أن الله لم يره

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi says the man lied about how much he had spent, imagining God did not see the amount; the verse warns that God knows it.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: إنه كان كاذبا في قوله أنفقت كذا وكذا، ولم يكن أنفق جميع ما قال

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says the eyes, tongue, and lips are conspicuous blessings that remind a person to give thanks.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة: نعم الله متظاهرة يقررك بها كيما تشكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith presents God telling Adam’s child to close the lips when the tongue seeks the forbidden, shut the eyes when sight seeks it, and likewise restrain the sexual organ.
rows.anchor: وجاء في الحديث: أن الله عز وجل يقول: ابن آدم إن نازعك لسانك فيما حرمت عليك

rows.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
rows.claim: Most commentators say the two high paths are good and evil, truth and falsehood, or guidance and error, as in the verse that calls people either grateful or ungrateful.
rows.anchor: قال أكثر المفسرين: طريق الخير والشر، والحق والباطل، والهدى والضلالة

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Muhammad b. Kaʿb reports Ibn Abbas’s interpretation of the two paths as the two breasts; saʿid b. al-Musayyab and al-Dahhak share it.
rows.anchor: وقال محمد بن كعب عن ابن عباس: "وهديناه النجدين" قال: الثديين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Najd is a road rising to a height.
rows.anchor: والنجد: طريق في ارتفاع

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd and a group take failure to climb the obstacle as failure to spend wealth on freeing slaves and feeding the hungry, better uses than spending to oppose Muhammad.
rows.anchor: يقول: فهلا أنفق ماله فيما يجوز به من فك الرقاب وإطعام السغبان

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada says the obstacle is a metaphor for struggling against the self, desire, and Satan through good works; to fail to climb is to avoid the hardship of freeing and feeding.
rows.anchor: لم يحمل على نفسه المشقة بعتق الرقبة ولا طعام، وهذا معنى قول قتادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading simply says the person did not enter or pass the obstacle; in another metaphor, sins weigh like a steep barrier, crossed by freeing a slave and feeding someone hungry.
rows.anchor: وقيل: "فلا اقتحم العقبة" أي لم يقتحمها ولا جاوزها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God proportioned the soul’s creation and its limbs; Ata says ‘soul’ here means all that God created of jinn and humans.
rows.anchor: عدل خلقها وسوى أعضاءها. قال عطاء: يريد جميع ما خلق من الجن والإنس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, in a report through Ali b. Abi Talha, says God showed the soul good and evil.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس في رواية علي بن أبي طلحة: 193/ب بين لها الخير والشر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: In another report, Ibn Abbas says God taught the soul obedience and disobedience.
rows.anchor: وقال في رواية عطية: علمها الطاعة والمعصية

rows.speaker: الكلبي عن أبي صالح عن ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi reports from Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas that God made the soul recognize good and what evil to avoid.
rows.anchor: وروى الكلبي عن أبي صالح عنه: عرفها ما تأتي من الخير وما تتقي [من الشر] (1)

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿid b. Jubayr interprets the wording as binding the soul to its evil and piety.
rows.anchor: وقال سعيد بن جبير: ألزمها فجورها وتقواها

rows.speaker: ابن زيد والزجاج
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says God placed both tendencies in the soul by enabling piety and abandoning it to evil; al-Zajjaj chooses this as divine enabling and withdrawal, showing that God creates piety in believers and evil in unbelievers.
rows.anchor: قال ابن زيد: جعل فيها ذلك، يعني بتوفيقه إياها للتقوى، وخذلانه إياها للفجور

rows.speaker: عمران بن حصين
rows.claim: Imran b. Husayn asks whether human striving follows prior decree or newly established proof; a visitor asks the Prophet and he answers that deeds are decreed, and God prepares each person for one of two abodes, citing this verse.
rows.anchor: عن الأسود الديلي قال: قال لي عمران بن حصين: أرأيت ما يعمل الناس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is the oath’s answer: a soul succeeds when God reforms and cleans it of sin and enables it to obey.
rows.anchor: وهذا موضع القسم، أي فازت وسعدت نفس زكاها الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The soul God misleads and corrupts is ruined.
rows.anchor: أي خابت وخسرت نفس أضلها الله فأفسدها

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan instead makes the person the subject: one succeeds by purifying and directing the soul to obedience, and loses by ruining it through sin.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: معناه قد أفلح من زكى نفسه فأصلحها وحملها على طاعة الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dassa derives from repeated hiding (dassasa); the second sīn becomes yāʾ, and the sense is to abase or conceal the soul through unbelief and disobedience.
rows.anchor: أصله: دسسها من التدسيس، وهو إخفاء الشيء، فأبدلت السين الثانية ياء

rows.speaker: زيد بن أرقم
rows.claim: Zayd b. Arqam reports that the Prophet sought refuge from incapacity, laziness, miserliness, cowardice, worry, and grave punishment, asking God to grant and purify the soul’s piety and protect from other spiritual failings.
rows.anchor: عن زيد بن أرقم قال: لا أقول لكم إلا ما قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم لنا: "اللهم إني أعوذ بك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thamud’s rebellion and aggression drove them to deny the truth.
rows.anchor: بطغيانها وعدوانها، أي الطغيان حملهم على التكذيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The most wretched man rose and hurried to slaughter the she-camel; he was Qudar b. Salif, short, fair-haired, and blue-eyed.
rows.anchor: وهو: قدار، بن سالف، وكان أشقر أزرق [العينين] (1) قصيرا قام لعقر الناقة

rows.speaker: عبد الله بن زمعة
rows.claim: Abd Allah b. Zamʿa reports that the Prophet described the camel’s killer as a powerful, vicious man of standing among his people, like Abu Zamʿa.
rows.anchor: عن أبيه أنه أخبره عبد الله بن زمعة أنه سمع النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم يخطب وذكر الناقة والذي عقرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Messenger is Salih, who warns them to protect God’s she-camel from being hamstrung.
rows.anchor: صالح عليه السلام، {ناقة الله} أي احذروا عقر ناقة الله

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj construes ‘God’s camel’ as an object of an implied command: leave the she-camel and her allocated drinking turn alone.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: منصوب على معنى: ذروا ناقة الله، {وسقياها} شربها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They rejected Salih and hamstrung the she-camel.
rows.anchor: يعني صالحا، {فعقروها} يعني الناقة

rows.speaker: عطاء ومقاتل
rows.claim: Ata and Muqatil gloss damdama as God destroying them; al-Muʾarrij specifies total annihilation.
rows.anchor: قال عطاء ومقاتل: فدمر عليهم ربهم فأهلكهم. قال المؤرج: الدمدمة إهلاك باستئصال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their sin was denying the messenger and hamstringing the camel; God leveled punishment over all, leaving no one alive.
rows.anchor: بتكذيبهم الرسول وعقرهم الناقة، {فسواها} فسوى الدمدمة عليهم جميعا، وعمهم بها

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farraʾ says the whole nation was leveled, with punishment falling on young and old alike.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء: سوى الأمة وأنزل العذاب بصغيرها وكبيرها، يعني سوى بينهم

rows.speaker: أهل المدينة والشام
rows.claim: Medinan and Syrian readers begin the verse with faʾ, as in their codices; the remaining readers use wāw, matching their codices.
rows.anchor: قرأ أهل المدينة والشام: "فلا" بالفاء وكذلك هو في مصاحفهم، وقرأ الباقون بالواو

rows.speaker: الحسن وابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Hasan, also reported from Ibn Abbas through Ali b. Abi Talha, says God fears no consequence or liability from anyone for destroying them.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن: معناه: لا يخاف الله من أحد تبعة في إهلاكهم. وهي رواية علي بن أبي طلحة عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: الضحاك والسدي والكلبي
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, and al-Kalbi instead refer the fearlessness to the camel’s killer, with the clause moved ahead in sense: he rose without fearing the consequence.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك، والسدي، والكلبي: هو راجع إلى العاقر، وفي الكلام تقديم وتأخير
